front: [Chain: DAYCOUNT 1/4] Context: accrual period from 1 Jan 2026 to 1 Jul 2026 (a semi-annual period on a 5% coupon). Define ACT/360, ACT/365F, 30/360 (bond basis) and ACT/ACT ICMA, and give the year fraction each one produces for this period.
back:
Headline: a day count turns two dates into a year fraction \(\tau\). Four conventions dominate:
  • ACT/360: \(\tau = d/360\), actual days over 360. Used for USD and EUR money markets (SOFR, €STR, USD and EUR deposits and FRAs).
  • ACT/365F (Fixed): \(\tau = d/365\). Used for GBP money markets and SONIA, and for many sterling instruments.
  • 30/360 (bond basis): \(\tau = \dfrac{360(Y_2-Y_1)+30(M_2-M_1)+(D_2-D_1)}{360}\), with any day-of-month of 31 set to 30. Used for US corporate and agency bonds and many EUR fixed legs.
  • ACT/ACT (ICMA): \(\tau = \dfrac{d}{f\cdot D_{\text{quasi}}}\), where \(f\) is coupon frequency and \(D_{\text{quasi}}\) is the number of days in the quasi-coupon period. Used for UK gilts and US Treasuries.
Calculation for 1 Jan to 1 Jul 2026: actual days \(d = 181\). ACT/360 gives \(181/360 = 0.50278\). ACT/365F gives \(181/365 = 0.49589\). 30/360 gives \(180/360 = 0.5000\). ACT/ACT ICMA gives \(181/(2\times181)=0.5000\), because this period is itself the quasi-coupon period.
Used in the deck for: every accrual, coupon and money-market cash-flow card in this section, and the gilt clean/dirty cards.

front: [Chain: DAYCOUNT 2/4] Context: £100m notional at 5.00%, accrual 1 Jan 2026 to 1 Jul 2026 (181 actual days). Compute the interest under ACT/360 and under ACT/365F. Which is larger, and by how much?
back:
Headline: ACT/360 pays more interest than ACT/365F on the same rate, by a factor of \(365/360 = 1.01389\).
Computation:
ACT/360: \(100{,}000{,}000 \times 0.05 \times \dfrac{181}{360} = £2{,}513{,}889\).
ACT/365F: \(100{,}000{,}000 \times 0.05 \times \dfrac{181}{365} = £2{,}479{,}452\).
Difference: \(£34{,}437\) on one coupon, which is about 3.4bp of notional, or about 1.4% more interest.
Why it matters: a 5.00% ACT/360 rate is economically the same as 5.069% on ACT/365F (\(0.05\times365/360\)). Comparing a SOFR (ACT/360) swap with a SONIA (ACT/365F) swap at the same quoted rate therefore hides a yield gap of about 6.9bp.
Interviewer follow-up: a 90-day deposit of 10m at 5.00%: ACT/360 gives 125,000 and ACT/365F gives 123,288, a difference of 1,712. The desk must convert quotes to a common basis before comparing.
Used in the deck for: the SONIA vs SOFR/€STR basis cards and the money-market-to-bond-equivalent conversions.

front: [Chain: DAYCOUNT 3/4] Context: a US corporate bond pays a 6% semi-annual coupon, accrued from 15 Mar 2026 to 15 Jun 2026 on £/$100 face. Compute accrued under 30/360 and under ACT/365F, and state which one a US corporate desk uses and why it matters for the dirty price.
back:
Headline: 30/360 gives accrued of 1.50, and ACT/365F gives 1.5123. US corporates accrue on 30/360, so the accrued is 1.50 per 100 face.
Computation: 30/360 gives \(\dfrac{360\cdot0+30\cdot3+(15-15)}{360} = \dfrac{90}{360} = 0.25\) of a year, so accrued \(=6\times0.25 = 1.50\). ACT/365F gives \(92/365 = 0.25205\), so accrued \(=6\times0.25205 = 1.5123\). The difference is 0.0123 per 100 face.
Why the desk cares: the dirty price is clean plus accrued. A 0.012 mismatch on a 100 face trade is 1.2 per £10,000 face, enough to break a trade-level reconciliation or a credit-trade confirmation, so the conventions must be right in the trade system.
Interviewer follow-up: over a quarter, 30/360 always counts 90 days, while actual days run from 89 to 92, so ACT accrual wobbles around the 30/360 figure. The desk must know which one a trade uses before it compares two accruals.
Used in the deck for: dirty-price reconciliation of corporate bonds and the ASW/CDS-bond basis cards.

front: [Chain: DAYCOUNT 4/4] Context: a UK gilt with 4% semi-annual coupon, coupon dates 1 Jan and 1 Jul. Settlement is 15 Mar 2026, which gives 73 actual days since 1 Jan in a 181-day quasi-coupon period. Derive the ACT/ACT (ICMA) accrued interest per 100 face.
back:
Headline: accrued \(= 2.00 \times 73/181 = 0.8066\) per 100 face.
Derivation:
1. Coupon per period is \(C = 100 \times c / f = 100\times0.04/2 = 2.00\).
2. Under ICMA the accrual within a regular period is the fraction of the quasi-period elapsed: \(AI = C \times \dfrac{d_{\text{elapsed}}}{D_{\text{quasi}}}\).
3. Here \(d_{\text{elapsed}} = 73\) (1 Jan to 15 Mar) and \(D_{\text{quasi}} = 181\) (1 Jan to 1 Jul).
4. \(AI = 2.00 \times 73/181 = 0.80663\).
5. Dirty price \(=\) clean price \(+ 0.8066\).
Why the denominator is the quasi-period: ICMA measures accrual against the coupon period itself, so the accrued fraction runs from 0 to 1 across the coupon period regardless of how many calendar days it contains. This makes the accrued continuous in time with the coupon.
Where it breaks: for an irregular first or last coupon (long or short), the accrual is the sum of accruals over each quasi-coupon period that the bond spans, not one fraction. Using the actual days in a long first coupon can misstate accrued materially. Treasuries use ACT/ACT on a similar principle but with their own roll rules.
Used in the deck for: gilt dirty-price cards, ex-dividend cards and the gilt repo carry cards.

front: Which market uses which day count, and why does a 5.00% SONIA rate and a 5.00% SOFR rate not mean the same thing? Give the basis gap in bp.
back:
Answer: SONIA is ACT/365F and SOFR is ACT/360. A 5.00% SOFR rate is worth \(5.00\% \times 365/360 = 5.069\%\) on the SONIA basis, so the two quotes differ by about 6.9bp for the same economic rate.
Why it matters: a desk running a multi-currency curve (USD SOFR and GBP SONIA) must convert every quote to a common year fraction before bootstrapping or comparing. Ignoring this gives a systematic basis error of about 7bp at 5% and about 3bp at 2%, which is comparable to the edge on many relative-value trades.
Interviewer follow-up: the same issue arises for a T-bill (ACT/360 discount) and a Treasury note (ACT/ACT). Answer: you convert both to a bond-equivalent yield on the same basis before quoting a spread.
Used in the deck for: the SONIA/SOFR basis and bond-equivalent cards.

front: [Chain: COMP 1/4] Context: a 5.00% rate over 1 year. Define simple, annual, semi-annual and continuous compounding, and compute the one-year discount factor under each.
back:
Headline: compounding is the convention that maps a rate \(r\) to growth over time. Discount factor (DF) is the reciprocal of growth.
  • Simple (money-market style, one period): \(DF = \dfrac{1}{1+r\tau}\)
  • Annual: \(DF = (1+r)^{-T}\)
  • Semi-annual: \(DF = (1+r/2)^{-2T}\)
  • Continuous: \(DF = e^{-rT}\)
Computation for 5.00% over 1 year: simple \(=1/1.05 = 0.952381\) (same as annual). Semi-annual \(=1/1.025^2 = 0.951814\). Continuous \(=e^{-0.05}=0.951229\).
Ordering: for the same nominal rate, the more frequent the compounding, the larger the growth and the smaller the DF. Continuous is the upper bound.
Used in the deck for: converting between quoting conventions (COMP 2 and 3), and the DF-based pricing of swaps and bonds.

front: [Chain: COMP 2/4] Context: a 90-day USD deposit at 4.00% quoted on ACT/360 (simple). Give the DF over the 90 days and the equivalent rate on ACT/365F that pays the same interest.
back:
Computation:
\(DF = \dfrac{1}{1+0.04\times 90/360} = \dfrac{1}{1.01} = 0.990099\).
The interest is \(0.04\times90/360 = 1.0\%\) of notional. On ACT/365F the same interest needs a rate \(r_{365}\) with \(r_{365}\times 90/365 = 0.01\), so \(r_{365} = 0.04\times365/360 = 4.0556\%\).
Rule: a simple rate on ACT/360 converts to ACT/365F by multiplying by \(365/360\). Interest is preserved, so a 4.00% ACT/360 deposit is a 4.0556% ACT/365F deposit.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the continuous-compounded equivalent? Answer: over \(\tau = 0.25\), \(\ln(1.01)/0.25 = 3.980\%\) continuously compounded. The continuous rate is always the smallest of the three for the same growth, which is why a continuous quote looks low.
Used in the deck for: money-market-to-bond-equivalent conversions, the T-bill cards and the FRA settlement mechanics.

front: [Chain: COMP 3/4] Context: 5.00% annual effective, and the limit of \((1+r/n)^n\) as the compounding frequency \(n\) grows. Derive the continuous rate and show it converges to \(e^{r}\).
back:
Derivation:
1. Compounding \(n\) times a year at nominal \(r\) gives growth \((1+r/n)^n\).
2. Take logs: \(n\ln(1+r/n)\). Using \(\ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + \dots\) with \(x=r/n\), this is \(r - \dfrac{r^2}{2n}+\dots\).
3. As \(n\to\infty\), the log tends to \(r\), so the growth tends to \(e^{r}\).
4. For \(r=5\%\): \(n=1: 1.050000\), \(n=2: 1.050625\), \(n=12: 1.051162\), \(n=365: 1.051267\), limit \(1.051271\).
5. The continuous rate equivalent to 5.00% annual effective is \(\ln(1.05)=4.879\%\).
Where it breaks: the identity \(e^{r\tau}\approx 1+r\tau\) holds only to first order. For a money-market accrual of \(\tau=0.25\) at 5%, the simple and continuous factors differ by \(\approx r^2\tau^2/2 = 0.00008\), which is about 0.8bp of growth. Do not treat a simple rate as continuous at long tenors.
Used in the deck for: model-side discounting (HJM, short-rate and credit models use continuous rates) and the continuous-vs-annual DF comparison in COMP 4.

front: [Chain: COMP 4/4] Context: a 10-year discount factor at 5.00%. Compare semi-annual compounding (quote convention for many USD and GBP bonds) with continuous compounding (model convention). Which do you use for a bond price and which for a model, and what is the size of the difference?
back:
Computation: semi-annual \(DF = 1.025^{-20} = 0.610271\). Continuous \(DF = e^{-0.5} = 0.606531\). The difference is 0.003740, which is about 0.37 points on a par bond.
Answer: quote and settle a bond on its own periodic convention, which is semi-annual for the price-yield formula, because that is how coupons are paid. Use continuous compounding inside a model because discounting becomes \(\exp(-\int r\,dt)\), a clean exponential of the integrated short rate.
Trade-off: the 0.37-point gap is not a model error; it is the same rate on a different basis. Mixing the two in one curve, for example a semi-annual quote fed into a continuous bootstrap, produces a systematic curve bias of that size.
Interviewer follow-up: how would you convert a semi-annual zero to continuous? Answer: \(r_c = 2\ln(1+r_{s}/2)\), which for \(r_s=5\%\) gives 4.939%.
Used in the deck for: curve-building conventions, the bootstrap cards and the model-to-quote reconciliation.

front: [Chain: FRA 1/5] Context: a 3x6 FRA on a notional of 10m, fixed rate \(K=4.00\%\), period \(\tau = 0.25\) (90 days, ACT/360). On the fixing date the rate \(L\) sets at 4.50%. Define the FRA, who pays and receives, and compute the settlement amount.
back:
Headline: a FRA is an OTC agreement to exchange a fixed rate \(K\) for a floating rate \(L\) set at the start of a future period. Settlement is paid at the start of the period, discounted at the period's own rate.
Terms: the buyer receives \(L\) and pays \(K\). The seller does the reverse. A "3x6" FRA starts in 3 months and ends in 6 months.
Settlement formula at the start date:
\[ \text{Settle} = N\,\tau\,\frac{L-K}{1+\tau L}. \] The denominator is the discount for paying at the start of the period rather than the end.
Numbers: \(10{,}000{,}000\times0.25\times\dfrac{0.045-0.04}{1+0.25\times0.045}=£12{,}360.94\) (the same figure for 10m of any currency at these rates). The buyer receives this amount.
Used in the deck for: every floating-rate hedge with FRAs (FRA 4), the FRA-to-swap strip (FRA 5) and the forward-rate cards.

front: [Chain: FRA 2/5] Context: the discount factors to the FRA's start and end dates are \(DF(T_1) = 0.9900\) and \(DF(T_2) = 0.9800\), with \(\tau = 0.25\). Derive the fair (par) FRA rate \(F\) and the value of the 4.00% FRA from FRA 1 for the buyer.
back:
Derivation:
1. No-arbitrage: a dollar at \(T_1\) must grow at \(F\) to match the dollar that is rolled through the discount curve to \(T_2\). So \(DF(T_1)\,=\,DF(T_2)\,(1+\tau F)\).
2. Solve: \(F = \dfrac{1}{\tau}\left(\dfrac{DF(T_1)}{DF(T_2)}-1\right)\).
3. Numbers: \(F = \dfrac{1}{0.25}\left(\dfrac{0.99}{0.98}-1\right) = 4.0816\%\).
4. Value to the buyer at today's date, with \(K=4.00\%\) and \(N=10\text{m}\): \(V = N\,\tau\,(F-K)\,DF(T_2) = 10^7\times0.25\times0.000816\times0.98 = £2{,}000\).
Where it breaks: the formula uses one curve for both fixing and discounting. Under multi-curve (projection curve for \(L\), OIS curve for discounting), the fair rate is taken from the projection curve, while the value uses the discount curve. Using a single curve here produces a basis error of the same order as the spread between them.
Used in the deck for: FRA pricing, the forward-rate construction in the bootstrap, and FRA 5 (swap as a strip of FRAs).

front: [Chain: FRA 3/5] Context: the same 10m 3x6 FRA as before, with \(\tau=0.25\) and \(DF(T_2)=0.98\). Compute the PV01 (or DV01) of the FRA to a 1bp move in the forward rate, and explain why it is much smaller than a 6-month bond's DV01.
back:
Answer: the FRA's DV01 is \(N\,\tau\,DF(T_2)\times 0.0001 = 10^7\times0.25\times0.98\times0.0001 = £245\) per bp.
Why it is small: the rate exposure is only over the period \([T_1,T_2]\), so its sensitivity scales with \(\tau\), not with maturity. A 6-month bond exposed to a 1bp move in its yield has DV01 \(\approx N\,D_{mod}\,P\,0.0001\), with \(D_{mod}\approx0.5\), giving about \(10^7\times0.5\times0.0001\approx£500\), so the FRA is about half the bond's DV01 for the same notional and period. The FRA's exposure is to one forward rate over one period, while the bond's is to every coupon and the principal.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the DV01 of an FRA strip that hedges a swap? Answer: the sum of the individual FRA DV01s, which equals the swap's annuity-weighted DV01 when the strip is exact.
Used in the deck for: bucketed DV01 of FRA strips and the swap-DV01 cards.

front: [Chain: FRA 4/5] Context: a corporate borrower has a £50m floating loan that resets 3-monthly on SONIA-type compounding (taken as a 3m rate here) and wants to lock its 3-month cost at 4.20%. It buys a 3m FRA at \(K=4.20\%\) on \(\tau=0.25\). On the fixing date, \(L = 4.90\%\). Compute the FRA payoff and show that the effective interest is locked at 4.20%.
back:
Computation:
1. FRA payoff at the start date: \(50{,}000{,}000\times0.25\times\dfrac{0.049-0.042}{1+0.25\times0.049} = £86{,}441\), received by the borrower because the borrower buys the FRA (pays fixed, receives floating).
2. The loan's interest is paid at \(T_2\), so the FRA payoff must be rolled forward to \(T_2\) at the floating rate: \(86{,}441\times(1+0.25\times0.049) = £87{,}500\).
3. Loan interest at \(L\): \(50\text{m}\times0.049\times0.25 = £612{,}500\).
4. Net interest: \(612{,}500 - 87{,}500 = £525{,}000\), which equals \(50\text{m}\times0.042\times0.25\).
5. The effective rate is exactly \(K = 4.20\%\) regardless of the fixing.
Interviewer follow-up: what if the FRA is settled at \(T_1\) but the borrower's payment is at \(T_2\) without the roll? The borrower is short the \(1+\tau L\) factor, so the hedge is off by \(86{,}441\times0.01225 = £1{,}059\), a small but real basis.
Used in the deck for: hedge-accounting and corporate-treasury hedging cards and the FRA payoff discount mechanics.

front: [Chain: FRA 5/5] Context: a 2-year annual-pay swap, valued with discount factors \(DF(1)\) and \(DF(2)\). Show that the swap is a strip of two FRAs, and derive the par swap rate as the fixed rate that makes the strip value zero.
back:
Derivation:
1. Each swap period behaves like a FRA: the floating rate \(F_i\) is fixed at the start of period \(i\) and paid at \(T_i\), and the fixed rate \(K\) is paid on the same date. So the swap is FRA(0 to 1) plus FRA(1 to 2), both at fixed rate \(K\).
2. Value at inception with \(\tau=1\): \(V = \sum_i DF(T_i)\,(F_i-K)\).
3. Forward definition: \(F_i = \dfrac{DF(T_{i-1})}{DF(T_i)}-1\), so \(DF(T_i)F_i = DF(T_{i-1})-DF(T_i)\). The floating legs telescope to \(1-DF(T_n)\).
4. The fixed leg is \(K\sum_i DF(T_i)\). Setting \(V=0\) gives \(S = \dfrac{1-DF(T_n)}{\sum_i \tau\,DF(T_i)}\), the par swap rate.
5. Check: \(DF(1)=0.9615\) and \(DF(2)=0.9246\) give \(S=(1-0.9246)/(0.9615+0.9246)=3.998\%\), about 4.00%.
Where it breaks: the telescoping needs every forward to come from the same curve that discounts the cash flows. Under multi-curve (SOFR projection vs OIS discounting), the floating leg does not telescope to \(1-DF(T_n)\), and the swap rate differs from the FRA-strip rate by the basis.
Used in the deck for: the swap-rate and annuity derivation cards (the par rate as an annuity-weighted average of forwards) and the swap-curve bootstrap.

front: [Chain: YTM 1/4] Context: a 5-year 5% semi-annual bond, quoted clean at 98.00 on a coupon date (so accrued is zero). Define yield to maturity (YTM) and solve for it.
back:
Definition: YTM is the single discount rate \(y\), applied to every remaining cash flow, that makes the present value equal to the dirty price. It is the internal rate of return of holding the bond to maturity with every coupon reinvested at \(y\).
Equation (semi-annual, \(f=2\), 10 periods, coupon 2.50, redemption 100):
\[ 98 = \sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac{2.50}{(1+y/2)^k} + \frac{100}{(1+y/2)^{10}}. \] Solution: \(y \approx 5.4625\%\) on a semi-annual basis. In annual effective terms this is \((1+0.054625/2)^2-1 = 5.537\%\).
Reading it: the price is below par because the yield (5.46%) is above the coupon (5.00%). A bond trades at a discount exactly when its YTM exceeds its coupon, and at a premium when it is below.
Used in the deck for: yield quoting, the price-yield mental-math cards and the carry/roll cards that use YTM as the bond's return proxy.

front: [Chain: YTM 2/4] Context: a 5-year 4% annual-coupon bond bought at par, so its YTM is 4.00%. Assume the coupons are reinvested at 2.00% and the bond is held to maturity. What is the realised annual return, and why is it not the YTM?
back:
Computation: the coupons reinvested at 2% accumulate to \(4(1.02^4+1.02^3+1.02^2+1.02+1) = 20.82\). Add the 100 principal to get a terminal value of 120.82 per 100 invested. The realised annual return is \((1.2082)^{1/5}-1 = 3.85\%\), which is below the 4.00% YTM.
Why: the YTM assumes every coupon is reinvested at the YTM itself. A realised return equals the YTM only if the reinvestment rate equals the YTM.
Interviewer follow-up: which bond has no reinvestment risk? Answer: a zero-coupon bond held to maturity. Its only cash flow is at maturity, so its realised return equals its YTM exactly, with no reinvestment assumption.
Where it breaks: for callable or prepayable bonds the YTM is not the expected return at all, because the issuer's option truncates the cash flows. Use the option-adjusted yield (or yield to worst) instead.
Used in the deck for: the carry-and-roll cards (where the reinvestment rate matters) and the callable-bond cards.

front: [Chain: YTM 3/4] Context: the same 5-year 4% semi-annual bond, yield 5.00%, but settled 0.4 of a coupon period before the next coupon (so 0.6 of the period has elapsed). Derive the dirty and clean price using the fractional-period formula.
back:
Derivation:
1. Let \(w\) be the fraction of the current coupon period remaining to the next coupon. Here \(w=0.4\).
2. The \(k\)-th future coupon falls \(k-1+w\) periods from settlement, so discount it by \((1+y/f)^{-(k-1+w)}\).
3. Dirty price: \(P_{\text{dirty}} = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\dfrac{c/f\cdot 100}{(1+y/f)^{k-1+w}} + \dfrac{100}{(1+y/f)^{n-1+w}}\). With \(c=4\%\), \(f=2\), \(n=10\), \(y=5\%\), the result is 97.05.
4. Accrued (ICMA, periods elapsed = \(1-w = 0.6\)): \(AI = (c/f)\cdot100\cdot(1-w) = 2.00\times0.6 = 1.20\).
5. Clean price \(= 97.05 - 1.20 = 95.85\).
Check: on a coupon date (\(w=1\)) the formula reduces to the standard annuity expression with exponents \(1,2,\dots,n\).
Where it breaks: the formula uses periods, not days, so it is exact only for regular periods. For irregular coupons (long or short first period) the exponents become fractional for every cash flow, and the schedule must be built from actual dates.
Used in the deck for: settlement-date pricing, the clean/dirty conversions in the gilt and corporate cards and the futures invoice-price cards.

front: [Chain: YTM 4/4] Context: the 5-year 5% semi-annual bond from YTM 1/4. At a trial yield of 6.00%, its dirty price is 95.73 and its modified duration is 4.34. Take one Newton step towards the 98.00 target and compare with the exact YTM of 5.4625%.
back:
Derivation:
1. Newton update: \(y_1 = y_0 - \dfrac{P(y_0)-P^*}{P'(y_0)}\).
2. Derivative: \(P'(y) = -D_{\text{mod}}\,P\), here \(-4.34\times95.73 = -415.6\) per unit yield.
3. Step: \(y_1 = 0.0600 - \dfrac{95.73-98.00}{-415.6} = 0.0600 - 0.00545 = 5.455\%\).
4. Exact YTM is 5.4625%, so the one-step error is about 0.75bp.
Where it breaks: the step uses only the first derivative, which is the duration approximation. Its error grows with the square of the distance from the solution, because the convexity term is neglected. A second step, or a secant method, removes the error quickly. For a trial yield far from the solution (say 15%), the duration-based step can overshoot, so solvers bracket the root first.
Used in the deck for: yield solvers in the pricing code, and the convexity-correction cards.

front: <b>Context: the 5-year 5% bond at 98.00 has a current yield of 5.10%, a YTM of 5.46%, and a 2-point discount to amortise over five years. Break the YTM into income and pull to par, and state the approximate-yield formula.
back:
Current yield \(= C/P = 5/98 = 5.10\%\). This is income only.
Approximate yield: \(\text{YTM}\approx \dfrac{C + (100-P)/n}{(100+P)/2} = \dfrac{5.00+0.40}{99} = 5.45\%\), close to the exact 5.46% (semi-annual basis).
Decomposition: the gap between YTM and current yield is the pull to par. The 2-point discount adds 0.40 per year, which is about 0.4% of the price base, on top of the 5.10% income.
Why it matters: a discount bond's return relies on the price converging to par. Holding it at constant yield, the price rises about 0.4 per year through pull to par, and that is the carry the desk earns.
Used in the deck for: carry and roll-down cards and the premium-versus-discount bond cards.

front: [Chain: ZERO 1/3] Context: a 6-month zero at 3.60% (semi-annual compounding) and a 1-year par bond with a 3.80% semi-annual coupon priced at 100. Bootstrap the 1-year discount factor and the 1-year zero rate.
back:
Step 1: \(DF(0.5) = 1/(1+0.036/2) = 0.982318\).
Step 2: par pricing: \(100 = 1.90\,DF(0.5) + 101.90\,DF(1)\). So \(DF(1) = (100 - 1.90\times0.982318)/101.90 = 0.963038\).
Step 3: semi-annual 1-year zero: \(z = 2\,(DF(1)^{-1/2}-1) = 3.802\%\). Continuous equivalent: \(-\ln DF(1) = 3.766\%\).
Intuition: a 1-year par bond's coupon is an average of the 6-month and 1-year zeros, so the 1-year zero sits a little above its 3.80% par coupon when the curve rises.
Used in the deck for: the bootstrap cards (BOOT chain) and the zero-curve interpolation cards.

front: [Chain: ZERO 2/3] Context: 2-year annual-pay par swap with discount factors \(DF(1)=0.9615\) and \(DF(2)=0.9246\) (a flat 4% curve, rounded). Derive the par rate from the discount factors.
back:
Derivation: a par swap has zero value, so the fixed leg equals the floating leg. The floating leg telescopes to \(1-DF(2)\), and the fixed leg is \(S\sum_i\tau\,DF(i)\). Setting them equal gives \(S = \dfrac{1-DF(T_n)}{\sum_i\tau\,DF(t_i)}\).
Numbers: \(S = \dfrac{1-0.9246}{0.9615+0.9246} = \dfrac{0.0754}{1.8861} = 3.998\%\), which is 4.00% with rounding.
Interpretation: the par rate is the annuity-weighted average of the forward rates, with weights \(\tau\,DF(t_i)/A\). This is the same identity used in the swap-rate derivations.
Interviewer follow-up: what is the annuity here? \(A = 0.9615+0.9246 = 1.8861\), which is what the PV01 of the fixed leg is built from.
Used in the deck for: par-to-zero conversion, swap annuities and PV01 of swaps.

front: [Chain: ZERO 3/3] Context: annual zero rates of 3%, 4% and 5% for 1, 2 and 3 years (upward sloping). Compute the 3-year par yield and compare it with the 3-year zero.
back:
Computation: \(DF(1)=0.970874\), \(DF(2)=0.924556\), \(DF(3)=0.863838\). Par yield \(=\dfrac{1-DF(3)}{DF(1)+DF(2)+DF(3)} = \dfrac{0.136162}{2.759268} = 4.935\%\).
Answer: the 3-year par yield is 4.93%, below the 5.00% 3-year zero. The par yield is an annuity-weighted average of the zeros, weighted by discounted cash flows. Early cash flows carry large weight and sit on lower zero rates, so the average is pulled down. On a rising curve, the par yield is below the longest zero, and on a falling curve it is above.
Where it breaks: the ordering depends on the whole shape. On a humped curve, where the 2-year zero is the highest, the 3-year par yield can sit above the 3-year zero. Always read curve shape from the zeros, not from par quotes.
Used in the deck for: curve-shape interpretation, the swap-versus-zero comparison and the bootstrap-error cards.

front: [Chain: SWAP_LEG 1/3] Context: a 2-year receive-fixed swap, 100m notional, fixed 4.00% paid annually, on a flat 4% annual curve at inception. Decompose the swap into a fixed-rate bond and a floating-rate note, and value the swap at inception.
back:
Decomposition: a receive-fixed swap is long a fixed-coupon bond and short a floating-rate note, both on the same notional. Value of the receiver \(= PV(\text{fixed leg}) - PV(\text{floating leg})\).
Value at inception: the fixed bond at 4% with 4% coupon is worth par (100). The floater is worth par at its reset date (SWAP_LEG 2/3). So the swap is worth \(100 - 100 = 0\) per 100 notional, which is why a par swap has zero value.
Why this matters: the swap has the same risk as a fixed bond minus a floater. Its DV01 is essentially the fixed bond's DV01, because the floater's DV01 is small (SWAP_LEG 3/3 and the floater-DV01 card).
Used in the deck for: swap valuation, the swap-as-bond decomposition in asset swaps and the swap-DV01 cards.

front: [Chain: SWAP_LEG 2/3] Context: a floating-rate note of notional \(N\) pays \(F_i\tau_i\) at each date \(T_i\), with \(F_i\) fixed at the start of its period \(t_{i-1}\). Show that the note is worth par on a reset date, and derive the value between resets.
back:
Derivation (on a reset date \(t_0\)):
1. PV of coupon \(i\) at \(t_0\): \(N F_i \tau_i DF(T_i)\).
2. Forward identity: \(F_i\tau_i\,DF(T_i) = DF(T_{i-1}) - DF(T_i)\), because the forward is defined off the same discount curve.
3. Sum the coupons: \(N\sum_i [DF(T_{i-1})-DF(T_i)] = N[DF(t_0)-DF(T_n)]\).
4. Add the principal: \(N\,DF(T_n)\). Total: \(N\,DF(t_0)\). At \(t_0\) the discount factor is 1, so the note is worth \(N\), par.
Between resets: the value at a date \(t\) is \((N + \text{accrued coupon}) \cdot DF(t,T_{\text{next}})\), where the coupon is already fixed.
Where it breaks: the telescoping needs the projection and discount curves to be the same. A floater with a quoted spread \(s\) is worth \(N + \text{PV}(s\cdot\text{annuity})\), and under multi-curve (SOFR projection vs OIS discounting) it trades slightly off par by the basis. A stale reset (index fixed earlier than the market value date) also moves it away from par.
Used in the deck for: the floater-DV01 and swap-decomposition cards and the multi-curve basis cards.

front: [Chain: SWAP_LEG 3/3] Context: the 2-year receive-fixed swap from SWAP_LEG 1/3 (100m, 4.00% fixed, flat 4% at inception, value zero). The flat curve rises 25bp to 4.25%. Recompute the discount factors, the annuity and the swap value, and state the DV01.
back:
Computation:
1. New DF: \(DF(1)=1/1.0425 = 0.959233\), \(DF(2)=1/1.0425^2 = 0.920\).
2. Annuity: \(A' = 0.959233+0.920 = 1.87936\).
3. New par rate: \(S' = 4.25\%\).
4. Receiver value: \(100\text{m}\times(0.0400-0.0425)\times1.87936 = -£469{,}840\). The receiver loses money because the fixed rate it receives is now below market.
5. DV01 (per bp, 100m): \(100\text{m}\times A'\times0.0001 = 18{,}794\). At the inception annuity of 1.8861 it is 18,861.
Sanity check: a linear estimate, \(25\times18{,}861 = 471{,}525\), is slightly larger than the exact \(469{,}840\). The 1.7k gap is the annuity falling as rates rise, which is the convexity of the swap.
Interviewer follow-up: why is the receiver's DV01 negative? Answer: a receiver is long fixed-rate cash flows, so its value falls when rates rise. A payer has the opposite sign.
Used in the deck for: swap MTM and DV01 cards, the PV01 of a swap, and the hedge-ratio cards.

front: Context: a 2-year floating-rate note has its next reset in 0.25 years and a notional of 100m. Estimate its DV01 per bp and compare it with the 2-year fixed receiver's DV01.
back:
Answer: the floater's DV01 is approximately \(N\times t_{\text{next reset}}\times0.0001 = 100\text{m}\times0.25\times0.0001 = £2{,}500\) per bp. The 2-year fixed receiver on the same notional has DV01 of about 18,861 per bp.
Why: a floater's value is fixed at par on each reset, so only the time from now to the next reset is exposed to a rate move. Its duration is therefore about the time to next reset, not the 2-year maturity.
Interviewer follow-up: what does this imply for a receiver swap hedged with a floater? Answer: the receiver's DV01 is almost all fixed-leg DV01, so the floater is not a hedge for it.
Used in the deck for: the swap decomposition, asset-swap DV01 and the floater-versus-fixed hedge cards.

front: [Chain: BP 1/3] Context: a 5-year 4% annual par bond at a 4% yield. Define a basis point, a price point, and the ticks used for US Treasuries. Then compute the DV01 per £100m for a 1bp move.
back:
Units:
  • 1 basis point (bp) = 0.01% = 0.0001 in yield.
  • 1 point = 1% of face value. A bond at 99.5 is 0.5 points below par.
  • US Treasury notes are quoted in 32nds of a point. "99-16+" means \(99 + 16/32 + 0.5/32 = 99.515625\) (the "+" is half a 32nd).
DV01 for the bond: the modified duration of a 5-year 4% annual par bond at 4% is 4.452. The price change per 1bp on 100 face is about \(4.452\times100\times0.0001 = 0.0445\). On £100m this is \(100\text{m}\times4.452\times0.0001 = £44{,}518\) per bp.
Interviewer follow-up: why is the DV01 of a 1bp move roughly proportional to duration? Answer: a bond's price sensitivity to a 1bp move is its duration multiplied by its price and by 0.0001, which is exactly the DV01 derived in BP 2/3.
Used in the deck for: every hedge-ratio and risk card that quotes DV01 in £ or $ per bp.

front: [Chain: BP 2/3] Context: a bond priced as \(P(y)=\sum_t CF_t(1+y)^{-t}\) (annual compounding, per 100 face). Derive the DV01 in terms of the modified duration.
back:
Derivation:
1. Differentiate: \(\dfrac{dP}{dy} = -\dfrac{1}{1+y}\sum_t t\,CF_t(1+y)^{-t}\).
2. Recognise the Macaulay duration \(D_{\text{mac}} = \dfrac{1}{P}\sum_t t\,PV_t\), so \(\dfrac{dP}{dy} = -\dfrac{D_{\text{mac}}P}{1+y} = -D_{\text{mod}}P\).
3. For a 1bp change \(\Delta y=0.0001\): \(\text{DV01} = -\dfrac{dP}{dy}\times0.0001 = D_{\text{mod}}\,P\times0.0001\).
4. Check on the 5-year par bond: \(4.452\times100\times0.0001 = 0.0445\) per 100 face, matching BP 1/3.
Where it breaks: the derivation is for a parallel yield shift of a single bond. For non-parallel curve moves, use key-rate DV01, and for bonds with embedded options the duration must be effective duration (price moves computed with the model).
Used in the deck for: DV01 for every bond and swap card, and the modified-duration cards.

front: [Chain: BP 3/3] Context: £100m of a 5-year 4% par bond (duration 4.452, DV01 £44.5k per bp) is replaced by a barbell of 2-year and 10-year 4% par bonds with the same DV01 (durations 1.886 and 8.111). Find the weights, compare convexity, and estimate the P&L of a 100bp move in each.
back:
Weights: equal duration requires \(w_2 D_2 + (1-w_2)D_{10} = D_5\), so \(w_2 = \dfrac{D_{10}-D_5}{D_{10}-D_2} = \dfrac{8.111-4.452}{8.111-1.886} = 0.588\). So 58.8% of the price is in the 2-year and 41.2% in the 10-year. Price-weighted DV01 is \(0.588\times1.886+0.412\times8.111 = 4.452\), the same as the bullet.
Convexity (years squared): bullet \(25.0\); barbell \(0.588\times5.41+0.412\times80.75 = 36.5\). The barbell is about 11.5 more convex for the same DV01.
100bp P&L per 100 face (price, convexity term \(\tfrac12 C P\Delta y^2\)):
Bullet: \(-4.452 + 0.125 = -4.327\).
Barbell: \(-4.452 + 0.182 = -4.270\).
Difference: about 0.057 per 100 face, so about £57k per £100m on a 100bp move, in favour of the barbell whichever way rates move.
Interviewer follow-up: is the barbell better? Answer: it is better only if you pay less for the convexity. A bullet at the same DV01 costs more in carry or in the market, so the trade-off is convexity against carry and roll.
Used in the deck for: butterfly and convexity trade cards and the carry-and-convexity trade-offs.

front: Context: a 5-year 5% annual-coupon bond priced at 4% yield (price 104.45). After one year, with the yield unchanged at 4%, the bond is a 4-year bond priced at 103.63. Compute the pull to par and the total return, and say what drives it.
back:
Computation: the price falls from 104.45 to 103.63, which is \(-0.82\) per 100 face. The coupon of 5.00 is received in the year, so the total return is \((5.00-0.82)/104.45 = 4.00\%\), exactly the yield.
Drivers: the premium bond's price decays towards par as its maturity shortens, with no change in yield. This is pull to par. Its size depends on the premium and the time left, and it reverses for a discount bond.
Interviewer follow-up: does the pull to par change with duration? Answer: it is largest for a short bond with a large premium and smallest for a long bond, so a premium bond with a 1-year maturity can lose most of its premium in a single year.
Used in the deck for: carry-and-roll cards, the total-return decomposition and the premium-versus-discount cards.

front: Context: a 2-year 4% annual-coupon par bond, yield moves up 50bp from 4.00% to 4.50%. Estimate the price change using modified duration and convexity, then compare with the exact price.
back:
Estimate:
  • Exact price at 4.50%: 99.064, so the change is \(-0.936\).
  • First-order (duration): \(-D_{\text{mod}}\,P\,\Delta y = -1.886\times100\times0.005 = -0.943\).
  • Convexity term: \(+\tfrac12 C P\Delta y^2 = +\tfrac12\times5.41\times100\times0.005^2 = +0.007\).
  • Sum: \(-0.943+0.007 = -0.936\), matching the exact price.
Why this matters: for a 50bp move, duration alone is accurate to about 0.7% of the move, and convexity is a rounding term on a 2-year bond. It matters much more on long bonds (PY 2 below).
Used in the deck for: P&L explain cards and the convexity-adjusted risk cards.

front: Context: a 10-year 4% annual-coupon par bond at a 4% yield. Rates rally 25bp to 3.75%. Estimate the price change using DV01 and convexity, and compare with the exact price.
back:
Estimate:
  • Exact price at 3.75%: 102.053, so the change is \(+2.053\).
  • First-order: \(D_{\text{mod}}\,P\,|\Delta y| = 8.111\times100\times0.0025 = +2.028\).
  • Convexity: \(\tfrac12\times80.75\times100\times0.0025^2 = +0.025\).
  • Sum: \(2.028+0.025 = 2.053\).
Takeaway: on a 10-year bond the convexity term is about 1.2% of the first-order move for a 25bp rally, and it always adds to the price whichever way yields move. This is why long bonds are worth owning in volatile rates markets, all else equal.
Used in the deck for: the bond convexity cards and the P&L-attribution cards.

front: [Chain: TBILL 1/3] Context: a 91-day US T-bill quoted at a 4.00% discount rate on ACT/360. Compute the price per 100 face.
back:
Computation: the discount rate applies to face value, so \(P = 100\left(1-0.04\times\dfrac{91}{360}\right) = 100\times(1-0.010111) = 98.9889\).
Answer: the bill is priced at 98.9889 per 100 face. The 4.00% is a discount rate, not a yield.
Used in the deck for: the bill-yield conversions (TBILL 2 and 3) and the repo-versus-bill comparison.

front: [Chain: TBILL 2/3] Context: the same 91-day bill, price 98.9889 per 100 face. Compute the bond-equivalent yield (365-day basis) and the money-market yield (ACT/360 basis).
back:
Computation:
Bond-equivalent yield (365 basis): \(\text{BEY} = \left(\dfrac{100}{P}-1\right)\dfrac{365}{91} = 4.0970\%\).
Money-market yield (360 basis): \(\text{MMY} = \left(\dfrac{100}{P}-1\right)\dfrac{360}{91} = 4.0409\%\).
Why the discount rate understates the return: the discount rate is earned on the face value, but the investor pays the price \(P\), which is smaller, so the same money earns a higher percentage on the price. The BEY is that percentage, quoted on a 365-day year.
Used in the deck for: the T-bill-to-repo comparison (TBILL 3) and the quoting-basis cards.

front: [Chain: TBILL 3/3] Context: the same 91-day bill at BEY 4.0970%, against a 4.00% repo on ACT/360 for the same 91 days. Put both on the same basis and say which earns more, and by how much.
back:
Like-for-like comparison: convert the 4.00% ACT/360 repo to the 365-day basis: \(4.00\%\times365/360 = 4.0556\%\).
Result: the bill's BEY of 4.0970% exceeds the repo's 4.0556% by about 4.1bp, on the same basis and the same term. A desk that buys the bill and finances it at the 4.00% repo rate earns about 4.1bp of carry before any price move.
Caveat: the comparison is pre-financing and pre-haircut. A real trade must include the bill's repo rate (which may differ from the 4.00% GC rate), settlement, and the cost of the balance sheet.
Used in the deck for: the bill-repo basis cards and the carry-on-cash-bond cards.

front: Context: a 3-month SOFR futures contract is quoted at 95.50. Explain what rate the price implies, how the contract settles, and what its DV01 is per contract.
back:
Answer: the implied average rate is \(100-95.50 = 4.50\%\). The contract settles on the compounded average SOFR over the reference quarter, and it is margined daily.
DV01: the contract covers $1m for 0.25 years, so its DV01 is \(1{,}000{,}000\times0.25\times0.0001 = \$25\) per bp per contract.
Caveat: because the contract is margined daily, its implied rate differs from the forward FRA rate by a convexity adjustment, which grows with the square of the time to expiry and with rate volatility.
Used in the deck for: the futures-strip and convexity cards, and the hedge-ratio cards that convert DV01 to contract counts.

front: [Chain: FWD 1/3] Context: 1-year zero at 4.00% and 2-year zero at 4.50%, both annually compounded. Derive the 1-year forward rate that starts in 1 year, and compute it.
back:
Derivation: no arbitrage requires \((1+z_2)^2 = (1+z_1)(1+f_{1,2})\), so \(f_{1,2} = \dfrac{(1+z_2)^2}{1+z_1}-1\).
Computation: \(f_{1,2} = \dfrac{1.045^2}{1.04}-1 = 5.0024\%\).
Interpretation: the forward is above both zeros because the curve is upward sloping. The 2-year zero is an average of the 1-year zero and the forward, so a higher forward is needed to lift the average from 4.00% to 4.50%.
Used in the deck for: forward-rate construction in the bootstrap and the FRA pricing cards.

front: [Chain: FWD 2/3] Context: the same 1-year and 2-year zeros, but now quoted continuously compounded (4.00% and 4.50%). Derive the continuously compounded forward and compare it with the annual-compounding answer from FWD 1/3.
back:
Derivation: \(e^{2z_2} = e^{z_1}e^{f}\), so \(f = 2z_2 - z_1\) in general \(f_{1,2} = \dfrac{z_2T_2 - z_1T_1}{T_2-T_1}\).
Computation: \(f = 2\times4.50\% - 4.00\% = 5.00\%\).
Comparison: the annual-compounding forward is 5.0024% and the continuous forward is 5.00%. These are not a contradiction: the inputs are the same numerals (4.00% and 4.50%) but represent different rates on different bases, so each forward is correct on its own convention. Never compare a forward from one convention with a zero from another.
Where it breaks: the linear formula is exact for continuous rates. Converting a forward quoted on one convention to another requires the conversion of both zeros first.
Used in the deck for: model-side forward curves (HJM, short-rate) and the convention-conversion cards.

front: [Chain: FWD 3/3] Context: discount factors \(DF(0.5)=0.98\) and \(DF(0.75)=0.97\), so the 3-month forward rate starting in 6 months (\(\tau=0.25\)) is \(F=(0.98/0.97-1)/0.25 = 4.124\%\). Compute the change in the forward for a 1bp change in \(DF(0.75)\), and explain the result.
back:
Computation: \(\dfrac{\partial F}{\partial DF_2} = -\dfrac{DF_1}{\tau\,DF_2^2} = -\dfrac{0.98}{0.25\times0.9409} = -4.17\). A 1bp (0.0001) change in \(DF_2\) moves \(F\) by \(-4.17\times0.0001 = -0.0417\%\), which is about 4.2bp.
Answer: a 1bp error in a discount factor becomes about a 4bp error in a 3-month forward, a multiplier of \(1/\tau = 4\) and a little more from the \(DF_2\) level.
Interviewer follow-up: how does this scale with the period? Answer: the forward's sensitivity to the DF is \(1/\tau\), so short-period forwards are very sensitive to a stale or noisy discount factor. This is why the bootstrap is done at pillar tenors and not on 3-month forwards alone.
Used in the deck for: the bootstrap-error cards and the forward-rate noise cards.

front: The ACT/360 to ACT/365F conversion factor is {{c1::365/360 = 1.0139}}, so a 5.00% ACT/360 rate is {{c2::5.069%}} on ACT/365F, with the same interest.
back: Interest is preserved: the rate scales by \(365/360\). Between SONIA (ACT/365F) and SOFR (ACT/360), a 5.00% quote is about 6.9bp apart on a common basis.

front: US corporate bonds accrue on {{c1::30/360}}, US Treasuries on {{c2::ACT/ACT}}, and UK gilts on {{c3::ACT/ACT ICMA}}.
back: Over one quarter, 30/360 always counts 90 days, while actual days run from 89 to 92. The accrual convention therefore changes the dirty price on a fixed trade by a small but reconcilable amount.

front: A continuously compounded rate \(r\) over \(T\) gives discount factor \(\exp(-rT)\), while a simple rate over \(\tau\) gives \(1/(1+r\tau)\). The two differ by about {{c1::\(r^2\tau^2/2\)}} for small \(r\tau\).
back: At 5% and \(\tau=0.25\), the difference is about 0.8bp of growth. The approximation is first order, so the gap grows with the square of \(r\tau\).

front: The par yield of a bond priced at par equals its {{c1::coupon}}. On an upward-sloping zero curve, the par yield is {{c2::below}} the zero rate at the same maturity.
back: The par yield is an annuity-weighted average of the zeros, so it is pulled towards the shorter zeros. See ZERO 3/3 for the numbers.

front: A floating-rate note is worth {{c1::par}} on a reset date, ignoring spread and discount basis. Its DV01 is approximately {{c2::N times time to next reset times 0.0001}}.
back: For N = 100m and 0.25 years to the next reset, the DV01 is about £2,500 per bp. The floater is nearly DV01-free compared with a fixed leg of the same maturity.

front: US T-bills are quoted on a {{c1::discount}} basis with {{c2::ACT/360}} days, while the bond-equivalent yield uses a {{c3::365}}-day year.
back: For the 91-day bill at a 4.00% discount rate, the price is 98.9889, the BEY is 4.0970% and the money-market yield is 4.0409%. See TBILL 1/3 and 2/3.

front: A 3-month SOFR futures price of 95.50 implies an average rate of {{c1::4.50%}}, and each contract has a DV01 of {{c2::$25 per basis point}}.
back: The DV01 is $1m times 0.25 times 0.0001, which is $25. The futures contract is margined daily, so its rate differs from the forward by a convexity adjustment.

front: An FRA fixes its rate at {{c1::the start of the period}}. It settles {{c2::at the start of the period}}, with the payment discounted by {{c3::\(1+\tau L\)}}.
back: Settlement amount \(= N\tau(L-K)/(1+\tau L)\). Paying at the start rather than the end is why the denominator appears. See FRA 1/5.

front: A 2-year annual-pay swap on a flat 4% curve has annuity {{c1::1.8861}}, so its DV01 is about {{c2::18,861}} per bp on 100m notional.
For the 2-year 4% annual par bond at 4%, the Macaulay duration is 1.9615, so the modified duration is {{c1::1.886}}, which equals {{c2::Macaulay divided by (1 + y)}}.
back: Modified duration is the Macaulay duration divided by \(1+y\) for annual compounding. This is the duration used in the DV01 derivation (BP 2/3).

front: A 4.00% simple rate over 90 days on ACT/360 is equivalent to a continuously compounded rate of {{c1::3.980%}} over the same period.
back: Continuous rate \(= \ln(1+0.04\times0.25)/0.25 = \ln(1.01)/0.25 = 3.980\%\). The continuous rate is always the lowest of the equivalents for the same growth.
